title: For clinicians and pharmacists
intro: What GAMSA offers prescribers, nurses and pharmacists who care for trans and gender diverse people: the injection training package, the pharmacist stock register, and the Australian prescribing and PBS references the patient pages are built on.

body: A free package for clinics giving the long-acting testosterone injection by the ventrogluteal route: a standard operating procedure and training guide, a one-page treatment-room card, a competency checklist, an adverse event form and a clinic audit tool. It was checked against the Australian Product Information for Reandron 1000 and Testosterone ADVZ 1000, a UK manufacturer's administration guidance for the same formulation, SA Health's ventrogluteal brochure, the SESLHD intramuscular injection guideline and the ASCIA anaphylaxis guideline. All five documents are version 2.4 (31 October 2026), and each has a document ID, an amendment table and a next review date (24 October 2027). Version 2.4 asks for observation for at least 30 minutes after each injection, and recommends, but does not require, a pregnancy test before each injection for anyone who could become pregnant, because testosterone must not be used in pregnancy [1]. Download it from the [testosterone undecanoate page](#/med/testosterone-undecanoate#sec-med-9). To report an error in the training documents, the [feedback page](#/feedback) is preferred; you can also email gamsaenquiries@gmail.com.

Registered pharmacists can post what is on their shelves. Each registration number is checked once against the AHPRA register; after that, reports publish immediately and show on the supply page and on each medicine page for 14 days. [Post a report](#/pharmacy-reports).
Points that come up most with gender-affirming scripts, with the page on this site that patients are reading:
list: Brand substitution and Serious Scarcity Substitution Instruments (SSSIs): check the [supply page](#/supply) for the current TGA position on each affected product before telling a patient nothing is available.
PBS Authority wording for testosterone does not describe gender-affirming use; the prescriber's indication wording is explained in the [costs guide](#/costs#sec-costs-7).
60-day prescriptions apply to several of these medicines and halve the counter cost; see the [costs guide](#/costs#sec-costs-4).

Closing the Gap: eligible Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients are registered once, by any PBS prescriber or Aboriginal Health Practitioner. No annotation on the script and no card are needed, and it applies at any pharmacy; see the [costs guide](#/costs#sec-costs-3).
Name and gender on the label: dispense under the name the patient uses where your software allows, and say so; the [pharmacy guide](#/pharmacy) tells patients what to ask for.
Easy Read guides on [this site](#/easy) can be printed for patients with low literacy or English as a second language; TIS National on 131 450 for interpreters.
sections.note: Bicalutamide is not first-line for gender-affirming care: check liver function regularly, stop it for jaundice or ALT above 2 × the upper limit of normal, and note the new interstitial lung disease precaution [11, 12, 13]. Bicalutamide potentiates warfarin (monitor PT/INR closely and consider anticoagulant dose adjustment) and inhibits CYP3A4 (midazolam levels up to 80% higher): terfenadine, astemizole and cisapride are contraindicated, and use caution with other CYP3A4 substrates such as ciclosporin, calcium channel blockers, HIV antivirals and statins. Photosensitivity reactions are a rare adverse effect [11]. On hormones and PrEP? They do not interact. Australian guidelines suggest that anyone on hormones (including those with a vagina) should take PrEP daily rather than on-demand; keep up kidney function tests, especially with spironolactone [12]. Patient wording is in the doses guide for [bicalutamide](#/doses#sec-doses-2) and on the monitoring page for [PrEP and hormones](#/monitoring#sec-monitoring-4).

body: A one-table summary of the monitoring in the AusPATH standards of care (2026) and the Australian position statement (2019) [1, 2]. It is a prompt, not a protocol: the current standards and the Product Information set the detail, and individual risk changes the intervals.

head: When
Everyone
Estradiol-based therapy
Testosterone-based therapy
rows: History and examination; baseline full blood count, electrolytes and kidney function, liver function, estradiol and testosterone, LH and FSH, prolactin [1, 2]; fasting lipids and glucose [2], or in AusPATH lipids, HbA1c, fasting glucose and ECG if cardiovascular risk factors are present [1]; vitamin D and sexual health screening if indicated [1, 2]. Fertility, contraception, smoking and clot risk discussed [1].
Baseline liver function before cyproterone, with periodic monitoring during treatment [1]. Electrolytes before spironolactone; care with renal impairment or medicines that raise potassium [1, 2].
Full blood count: testosterone raises haematocrit [2]. Fasting lipids and glucose [2].
Review clinical progress and blood tests every 3 to 4 months [1] (3-monthly in the position statement [2]): effects, sex steroid levels, mood, adverse effects, preventive screening [2].

Trough estradiol where feasible: just before the next dose for tablets or gel; for patches, consider testing just before a new patch is applied [1]. Keep estradiol above 250 pmol/L; AusPATH sets no upper limit, while the position statement suggested 250 to 600 pmol/L [1, 2]. Total testosterone under 2 nmol/L if full suppression is wanted; judge spironolactone's effect clinically [1]. Electrolytes while on spironolactone; liver function while on cyproterone [1, 2].

Trough total testosterone, timed to the formulation: just before the long-acting injection, and not adjusted until after three injections; before application for 1% gel and 5% cream; 2 to 4 hours after for 2% gel; midway between injections, or as a peak and trough, for testosterone enantate and mixed esters [1]. Aim for the lower end of the male range, about 10 to 20 nmol/L trough [1]; other guidance: the position statement suggested 10 to 15 nmol/L [2]. Haemoglobin and haematocrit at each review [2]. With an SGLT-2 inhibitor, monitor haematocrit and haemoglobin: the Reandron 1000, Gonadron, Rejunon 1000 and Sustanon 250 PIs report an increased risk of erythrocytosis with the combination [3]; the warning is not yet in the Testosterone ADVZ 1000, Primoteston Depot, Testogel, Testavan, AndroForte 5 or AndroFeme 1 PIs [4].

Review 6 to 12 monthly once stable [2] (annually in the standards of care [1]). Cancer screening by the organs present, not by gender or hormone status [1, 2]. Bone density if risk factors, including sub-therapeutic hormone levels [2].
Same bloods as the first year, at the review interval [1, 2].
Same bloods as the first year. If haematocrit is above 0.5, exclude other causes such as smoking, sleep apnoea or an SGLT-2 inhibitor, then lower the dose or lengthen the interval [1, 2, 3].

sections.note: Blood test timing in patient terms is in the [monitoring guide](#/monitoring#sec-monitoring-1). Sources: AusPATH 2026 baseline and review sections and Tables 5 and 7 [1]; position statement sections on baseline investigations, monitoring and polycythaemia [2]. GnRH analogues (puberty suppression, or lowering testosterone in adults): androgen deprivation may prolong the QT interval. Weigh this with congenital long QT, heart failure, frequent electrolyte abnormalities or QT-prolonging medicines, correct electrolytes, and consider periodic ECG and electrolytes (Zoladex PI s4.4/4.5; the same warning is in the Eligard, Lucrin and Diphereline PIs) [5]. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SJS/TEN, and DRESS and AGEP with triptorelin) are reported with triptorelin and leuprorelin [6]. Mood changes and depression, sometimes severe (very rare suicidal ideation or attempts), are reported with GnRH agonists; monitor patients with known depression closely. Convulsions are reported, mostly with risk factors [10]. Other interactions that need monitoring: testosterone may increase ciclosporin levels and the risk of nephrotoxicity [7], and Prometrium may raise ciclosporin levels [8]; oestradiol lowers lamotrigine levels and may reduce seizure control, so review the lamotrigine dose when oestradiol is started, changed or stopped [9].

body: A printable one-page card on how PBS testosterone prescriptions are worded for gender-affirming care: the indication the Australian position statement tells prescribers to use, who has to be named on the application, and a line to say to the patient at the counter.
[Authority wording card, version 1.5 (31 October 2026): one page to print (PDF)](/clinicians/pbs-authority-wording-card.pdf)
Patients: the plain-language explanation is in the [costs guide](#/costs#sec-costs-7).

Wholesaler and TGA alerts reach pharmacies, but rarely prescribers or patients. GAMSA publishes an RSS feed of every gender-affirming medicine currently affected by a TGA shortage notice, rebuilt each morning from the same data as the supply page. The [shortage alerts page](#/alerts) lists the current notices and explains how to add the feed to a feed reader, Outlook or Teams so it updates itself.
The patient pages cite their sources on every page. The ones prescribers ask for most:

sections.h: How the data on this site is kept current
body: Supply status is read from the TGA shortages database every morning for every medicine listed. PBS co-payments, Safety Net thresholds, brand premiums, listings and substitutable brands are read from the PBS at the start of each month, just after the PBS schedule changes on the 1st. Medicine pages show the date they were last reviewed, and the footer of every page shows when supply and PBS figures were last checked. If you find an error, the [feedback page](#/feedback) reaches the author directly.
